content: Periodontal disease is a prevalent condition among adults in the United States, ranging from mild gum inflammation to severe damage to the soft tissues and bone that support the teeth. In advanced cases, tooth loss can occur. The progression of gum disease largely depends on the individual’s oral hygiene practices moving forward. Causes The human mouth contains a variety of bacteria that, along with mucus and food particles, form a sticky, colorless film called plaque on the teeth. Regular brushing and flossing can remove plaque, but if it is not adequately removed, it hardens into tartar, which cannot be eliminated by brushing alone. Tartar requires professional cleaning by a dentist or dental hygienist for removal. Pathophysiology Gingivitis When plaque and tartar remain on the teeth for extended periods, they become increasingly harmful. The bacteria in plaque cause inflammation of the gums, a condition known as gingivitis. This results in gums that are red, swollen, and prone to bleeding. Gingivitis is a mild form of gum disease and is typically reversible with consistent brushing, flossing, and professional dental cleanings. Importantly, gingivitis does not involve the loss of bone or connective tissue that supports the teeth. Periodontitis If gingivitis is left untreated, it can progress to periodontitis, which is characterized by inflammation around the teeth. In this condition, the gums recede from the teeth, forming pockets that become infected. The body’s immune response to the bacterial infection, combined with bacterial toxins, leads to the breakdown of bone and connective tissue that anchor the teeth. Without treatment, the supporting structures of the teeth are destroyed, potentially resulting in tooth loss. Risk Factors Several factors increase the risk of developing periodontal disease: Smoking: Smoking is one of the most significant risk factors for gum disease and can also reduce the effectiveness of treatment. Hormonal changes in women: Hormonal fluctuations can make gums more sensitive and susceptible to gingivitis. Diabetes: Individuals with diabetes are at a higher risk of infections, including gum disease. Other illnesses and treatments: Conditions such as AIDS and cancer, along with their treatments, can negatively impact gum health. Medications: Certain medications reduce saliva production, which normally protects the mouth, making it more vulnerable to infections. Others can cause abnormal gum tissue overgrowth, complicating oral hygiene. Genetic predisposition: Some individuals are genetically more susceptible to severe gum disease. Epidemiology and Demographics Signs of gum disease typically appear in individuals in their 30s or 40s, with men being more commonly affected than women. While teenagers rarely develop periodontitis, they may experience gingivitis. The disease often arises when plaque accumulates along and beneath the gumline. Natural History, Complications, and Prognosis Periodontal disease has been associated with other systemic health conditions, though causation has not been definitively established. For example, studies suggest that individuals with gum disease may have a higher likelihood of developing heart disease or experiencing difficulty managing blood sugar levels. Additionally, women with gum disease may have an increased risk of delivering preterm, low-birth-weight babies. Further research is needed to determine whether gum disease directly contributes to these conditions or if the association is coincidental. It is also unclear whether treating gum disease can prevent the development of these systemic health issues. Symptoms Common symptoms of periodontal disease include: Persistent bad breath Red or swollen gums Tender or bleeding gums Pain during chewing Loose teeth Tooth sensitivity Receding gums or teeth that appear longer Physical Examination During a dental examination, the gums are assessed for signs of inflammation. In healthy gums, pocket depths range from 1 to 3 millimeters. This procedure is typically painless. Diagnostic Studies Dental x-rays may be taken to evaluate bone loss associated with periodontal disease. Treatment Patients with advanced gum disease may be referred to a periodontist, a specialist in diagnosing and treating periodontal conditions. The primary goal of treatment is to control the infection. The specific treatment plan depends on the severity of the disease and requires the patient’s commitment to maintaining good oral hygiene. Behavioral changes, such as quitting smoking, may also be recommended to improve treatment outcomes. Deep Cleaning: Scaling and Root Planing Scaling involves removing tartar from above and below the gumline, while root planing smooths rough areas on the tooth roots to eliminate bacteria and promote healing. In some cases, lasers may be used to remove plaque and tartar, resulting in less bleeding and discomfort compared to traditional methods. Medications Medications may be used alongside scaling and root planing but are not a substitute for surgical intervention in advanced cases. Examples include: Prescription antimicrobial mouthrinse: Chlorhexidine-based rinses are used to control bacteria, particularly after gum surgery or during gingivitis treatment. Antiseptic chip: A gelatin chip containing chlorhexidine is placed in periodontal pockets after root planing, releasing the medication over time. Antibiotic gel: Doxycycline-containing gel is applied to periodontal pockets to control bacteria and reduce pocket size. Antibiotic microspheres: Minocycline-loaded microspheres are inserted into pockets, releasing the antibiotic gradually. Enzyme suppressant: Low-dose doxycycline tablets inhibit destructive enzymes that break down gum tissue. Oral antibiotics: Short-term antibiotic courses may be prescribed for acute or persistent infections. Surgery Flap Surgery If deep pockets and inflammation persist after non-surgical treatments, flap surgery may be necessary. This procedure involves lifting the gums to remove tartar deposits and then suturing the gums back in place to fit snugly around the teeth. Post-surgery, the gums heal and tighten around the teeth, which may make the teeth appear longer. Bone and Tissue Grafts In cases of significant bone or gum tissue loss, grafting procedures may be recommended. Bone grafts, using natural or synthetic materials, promote bone regeneration. Guided tissue regeneration involves placing a mesh-like material between the bone and gum tissue to encourage regrowth of bone and connective tissue. Growth factors may also be used to stimulate natural bone regeneration. For gum tissue loss, soft tissue grafts using synthetic material or tissue from another part of the mouth can cover exposed tooth roots. Prevention To prevent periodontal disease: Brush teeth twice daily with fluoride toothpaste. Floss regularly to remove plaque between teeth. Use dental tools recommended by a professional, such as special brushes or picks. Visit the dentist regularly for check-ups and professional cleanings. Avoid smoking.
